title: What Massachusetts's Portrait of a Learner Gets Right (and New York's Doesn't) -and-new-yorks-doesnt
author: Coffey, Meredith
source: The Education Gadfly / Fordham Institute (fordhaminstitute.org), September 10, 2026
summary: Meredith Coffey compares two states' 'portrait of a graduate' initiatives and argues Massachusetts has found a workable model where New York has not. Her central claim is that a portrait framework only matters insofar as it changes concrete graduation requirements, and Massachusetts pairs its aspirational competencies with state-designed end-of-course exams, district-scored culminating experiences, and postsecondary-planning requirements, while New York leaves assessment methods and scoring almost entirely to individual teachers. She uses the Massachusetts MCAS graduation-requirement repeal as a parallel to New York's exit-exam rollback to show both states faced similar political pressure but responded very differently. The piece closes by praising Massachusetts's five-year runway to build out the details as evidence-based caution, contrasted with New York's vaguer, faster timeline affecting 860,000 students.
points: A 'portrait of a graduate' is only as meaningful as the graduation requirements it's actually tied to — competency language alone changes nothing.
Pairing broad aspirational competencies with state-designed, state-scored end-of-course exams preserves comparability that portfolio- or presentation-based assessment can't guarantee.
Letting individual teachers score open-ended 'demonstrations' (essays, performances, portfolios) against the same rubric risks wildly inconsistent judgments of the same competency.
A longer implementation runway (Massachusetts's 2031 vs. New York's 2029) is treated as a sign of more careful policy design, not just delay.
quotes: Since then, portraits of a graduate (or, sometimes, of a learner) have spread to at least 26 states, plus many more districts. The rationales vary—student disengagement, misalignment with evolving workforce demands, equity concerns—but the final product is typically a list of broad "competencies" that schools are meant to cultivate in each student.

The state EOC exam requirement is arguably where Massachusetts's proposal differs most from New York's. Two years ago, Massachusetts voters eliminated the state's much-lauded MCAS test as a graduation requirement—much like the Board of Regents has done to New York's erstwhile exit exams—but the Bay State hasn't abandoned the concept of a consistent, externally validated measure of student learning.

With EOC assessments baked into the graduation requirement, Massachusetts will be far better equipped to identify where students and schools need more support, which is crucial for educational equity. And, as long as standards are set high enough, its proposed system will also ensure that all students are held to a high standard.

This is potentially a deft compromise: Stakeholders wanted students to demonstrate learning beyond traditional testing. The culminating experience allows some local discretion while ensuring consistency within districts.

Lest readers see New York's haziness as excusable, since full implementation won't occur until 2029, I'll observe that Massachusetts has until 2031. That gives the Bay State a full five years to develop materials, train educators, and fine-tune the details. There's just no excuse for New York to be building the plane while flying it when 860,000 high schoolers' educations are at stake every year.

In sum, the aspirational nature of portraits of a graduate needn't come at the expense of substantive graduation requirements—the stuff that actually shapes instruction and learning. States adopting portraits would do well to be a Massachusetts, not a Monet.
